examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Intersection of a Circle With the Y-Axis
examples.problem:
Find the $y$-intercepts of the circle $x^2+y^2+2x-2y= 8,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13959190/assets/8eb9a6488191e8cf8a5b6107f3501e7d01938cf071e77b75890d570fc99cbf7a.png)
examples.worked_solution:
We must have $x = 0$ at the $y$-intercepts. 

So, we need to substitute $x = 0$ into the equation of the circle and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2x-2y & =8 \\ (0)^{2}+{y}^{2}+2(0)-2y & =8 \\ {y}^{2}-2y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2y+1 & =8+1 \\ (y-1)^{2} & =9 \\ y-1 & =\pm 3 \\ y & =1\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercepts occur at  $(0,-2)$ and $(0,4).$

Find the $x$-intercepts of the circle $(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=8,$ shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts. 

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-3)^{2}+(0-1)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-3)^{2}+1 & =8 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =7 \\ x-3 & =\pm \sqrt{7} \\ x & =3\pm \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts occur at the points $(3-\sqrt{7},0)$ and $(3+\sqrt{7},0).$
